core: Film language as the evolving conventions through which moving-image works organize and communicate meaning
A first-pass method for describing visible and audible choices before interpreting their effects
The relationship among mise-en-scene, cinematography, editing, sound, and narrative
supporting: Framing, camera movement, lighting, shot duration, transitions, diegetic and nondiegetic sound
Distinguishing observation, inference, and a claim about a maker's intent
outOfScope: Detailed study of mise-en-scene, cinematography, shot types, editing, continuity editing, montage, sound, music, narrative, genre, representation, and production history
Claims that a formal choice has one universal meaning or proves a filmmaker's private intention
Technical production instruction or copyright clearance

claims.claim: Film language can be understood as evolving conventions and formal choices through which cinema communicates, rather than as a literal spoken language with fixed one-to-one translations.
Introductory analysis can attend to production design or mise-en-scene, cinematography, editing, sound, performance, and narrative organization.
Mise-en-scene concerns what is placed before the camera, including such items as objects, sets, and costumes.
A formal analysis can describe camera distance or movement, shot length and transitions, lighting, and relations among images before making an interpretation.
Sound analysis may distinguish sounds within the story world from nondiegetic sound such as a score, while also attending to dialogue, voiceover, noise, music, and silence.
A credible interpretation identifies specific formal evidence and is stronger when it states its limits instead of treating one technique as proof of a single meaning or intention.
Film conventions are historically developed and may be repeated, recombined, or changed across works and audiences.

correctionsNeeded: Replaced generic boilerplate with a sourced account of film language as formal conventions and choices.

sourceRecords.notes: Open textbook read at the canonical University of Arkansas Pressbooks page. It supports the description of cinematic language as historically evolving conventions and identifies production design, narrative, cinematography, editing, sound, and performance as core dimensions of film form. The lesson uses original synthesis only.
